extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, district and appellate judges, and Supreme Court certiorari reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: A Supreme Court petition challenging the permissibility of Rule 12(b)(6) dismissals based on 35 U.S.C. § 101 (patent-eligibility), arguing that factual assertions and the presumption of validity bar such dismissals at the pleading stage. The document frames procedural and substantive standards courts must apply when resolving §101 challenges on the pleadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 12(b)(6) pleading standard (Twombly/Iqbal)
rubrics_metrics.description: To survive a motion to dismiss, a complaint must contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face; pleadings require only a short and plain statement giving fair notice. When there are well-pleaded factual allegations, the court should assume their veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Bell Atl. v. Twombly and Ashcroft v. Iqbal. Courts must accept the plaintiff's factual allegations as true and draw reasonable inferences in favor of the pleader. Pleadings include documents attached thereto (Fed. R. Civ. P. 10(c)) and a court may consider matters subject to judicial notice, but may not impermissibly weigh competing factual assertions at the pleading stage. Anti-pattern: resolving factual disputes or weighing evidence on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 101 patent-eligibility framework (Alice/Mayo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject matter includes processes, machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter; judicial exceptions include laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas. The Alice two-step test applies: (1) determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept; (2) if so, consider the claim elements individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether additional elements transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Mayo and Alice. Courts must identify whether claimed subject matter is an abstract idea (Alice step one) and whether the additional claim elements add something significantly more (Alice step two). The opinions emphasize the need to examine the claims, specification, and relevant factual context when applying the two-step test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice step one may involve factual considerations (secondary evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Alice step one, factual evidence such as commercial success and industry praise can be relevant to whether the claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Data Engine Techs. (considering contemporaneous articles and industry acclaim to find claims not directed to an abstract idea). The guidance is that objective evidence showing the invention improved computer functionality or was praised by industry can weigh against a finding that the claims are abstract at step one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice step two factual inquiry (well-understood, routine, conventional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alice step two requires consideration of whether claim elements or their combination are 'well-understood, routine, [and] conventional'—a question of fact that may preclude resolution at the pleadings or summary judgment stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Aatrix, Berkheimer, BASCOM, and Apple. Courts should treat determinations about whether elements are conventional as factual issues requiring evidence; exemplary guidance includes considering whether prior art taught away, whether elements behaved unexpectedly, and whether the record shows innovation beyond generic computer implementation. Anti-pattern: declaring elements 'generic' solely from claim language without factual record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction / subsidiary factual findings (Teva)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper § 101 analysis often requires claim construction, and claim construction involves subsidiary factfinding; understanding claim scope requires consideration of relevant evidence, including the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Teva Pharm. USA v. Sandoz: ultimate claim construction is a question of law but may require subsidiary factual findings. Guidance: courts should not substitute their own unsourced factual beliefs about what a person of ordinary skill in the art would have known or considered routine when construing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 overlaps with factual inquiries like novelty (§102) and nonobviousness (§103)
rubrics_metrics.description: The § 101 patent eligibility inquiry can overlap with § 102 novelty and § 103 nonobviousness inquiries, and thus may involve similar factual determinations (state of prior art, nature of the advancement embodied in the invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Microsoft and Mayo. Practical implication: factual questions commonly resolved in patent examination and §§102/103 contexts (e.g., prior art, technological advancement) are also pertinent to §101 and should be treated under normal procedural standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity under 35 U.S.C. § 282(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent shall be presumed valid; the burden of establishing invalidity rests on the party asserting invalidity, which must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites § 282(a) and Microsoft v. i4i. The petition argues the presumption extends to patent-eligibility inquiries and that courts must respect it when adjudicating §101 challenges—i.e., invalidity/ineligibility should not be resolved at the pleading stage where statutory presumption and the clear-and-convincing standard apply. Anti-pattern: resolving eligibility against the patentee without meeting the clear-and-convincing standard or without considering the presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patent specification 'admissions' as evidence (Mayo limited application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit admissions or statements in the patent specification (e.g., that elements are 'well known in the art') can be used to support a finding of ineligibility, but Mayo relied on specific admissions and prior art representations within the patent itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Mayo. Guidance warns against overgeneralizing Mayo: mere use of terms like 'computer', 'database', or 'web page' in a specification is not an automatic admission that such elements were 'well-understood, routine, [and] conventional' at the time of the invention. Courts should require more specific, substantive admissions or extrinsic evidence before treating specification language as dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper materials to consider on Rule 12(b)(6) motions
rubrics_metrics.description: On a motion to dismiss courts may consider the complaint, the patent, documents attached to the complaint, and matters subject to judicial notice; however, courts should not resolve disputed factual issues or rely on extrinsic factual findings outside those proper documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Fed. R. Civ. P. 10(c) and cases permitting judicial notice. Guidance: A limited evidentiary record is appropriate at pleading stage; factual disputes requiring evidence should be deferred to summary judgment or trial. Anti-pattern: courts construing the specification to reach factual conclusions unsupported by the pleadings or properly-noticed materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations / objective indicia are relevant to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of patentability—commercial success, licensing, industry recognition, teaching away in the prior art—are relevant to the Alice analysis and help guard against hindsight reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Data Engine, Rapid Litigation Management, DDR Holdings, and Graham. Guidance: courts should consider contemporaneous articles, licensing activity, industry praise, and evidence that prior art taught away when assessing whether claims are more than an abstract idea or embody an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: When §101 may be resolved at the pleading stage (no plausible factual allegations to impede resolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may determine patent eligibility at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage only if there are no plausible factual allegations that would preclude such a resolution—i.e., when no plausible factual disputes exist that materially affect the §101 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects Federal Circuit practice as described in the opinion: 'patent eligibility can be determined at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage if there are no plausible factual allegations to impede such a resolution.' The petition criticizes ambiguous phrasing like 'plausible factual disputes' as inviting improper fact-weighing; guidance is to apply Rule 12(b)(6) strictly by accepting plaintiff's factual allegations and permitting discovery where factual disputes exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity challenges under §101 treated as fact-intensive and subject to evidentiary standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenges to patent eligibility under §101 are, in effect, invalidity challenges and may implicate the same evidentiary standards and factual issues as §§102 and 103 (e.g., presumption of validity, clear-and-convincing proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Versata, CLS Bank (concurring), Berkheimer, and Microsoft. Practical effect: defendants bear a heavy burden to prove invalidity/ineligibility and courts should not bypass normal procedural protections by resolving evidence-dependent disputes at the pleading stage.
